extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in Pearl Harbor inquiry and postwar policy
extracted.subtask_short: reporting Pearl Harbor hearings and Germany policy
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-1940s newspaper report covering the joint congressional Pearl Harbor investigation (testimony, procedures, missing records) and the State Department/Byrnes statement on U.S. economic policy toward postwar Germany. It summarizes testimony, controversies, and official policy standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locked-pouch procedure for intercepted messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Intercepted and decoded Japanese messages were taken to top officers of the War Department in a 'locked pouch.' Those entitled to receive the messages 'had a Key to the pouch and, under usual procedure, read the messages and returned them to the pouch which was then taken on to someone else.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes expected chain-of-custody for highly classified intercepts; the article notes controversy because records/copies 'can now be found' and files were missing, raising questions about adherence to the procedure and preservation of records.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Winds' (activating) message — existence and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Tokyo reportedly had a signal—phrases like 'East winds, raining' or a 'winds'/'winds execute' message—to indicate a break in relations and potential further action; whether such a broadcast was ever made is disputed and has been 'a subject of considerable controversy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee investigators, decoded-message sources, and witnesses differ — some say no record in War Department files, others cite rumors; the standard question is whether such a code broadcast was sent and received, which would signal imminent hostile action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification/withholding of 'magic' (code-cracking) material
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior War Department aides reportedly directed that code-cracking secrets ('magic') be withheld from the Army board; Lt. Gen. Joseph McNarney told staff officers to instruct witnesses not to discuss 'magic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects an expectation/procedure that highly sensitive cryptographic intelligence can be restricted by high-level direction; the article records that the Navy board did introduce 'magic' messages, creating inter-board inconsistencies and raising questions about who may control disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction in warnings to await an overt act
rubrics_metrics.description: By presidential direction, all War Department warnings sent to American commanders before Pearl Harbor 'contained instructions to wait for an overt act by Japan.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents a policy/procedural standard applied to overseas commanders—warnings were to be accompanied by explicit instructions limiting defensive action until an overt act occurred; Marshall testified this was the practice and that such wording influenced local alert decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alert-level protocol (No. 1 vs. No. 2/3) and appropriate response
rubrics_metrics.description: Alert No.1 (anti-sabotage alert) was distinguished from higher alerts (No.2/3) implying increased readiness against aerial assault; Gen. Short testified he placed forces on No.1 because he did not think an air assault was likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats the choice of alert level as evaluative: whether No.1 was appropriate given the intelligence and transmissions from Washington; testimony emphasizes how War Department responses (or lack thereof) affected local decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-of-communication and recordkeeping for intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages were routinely sent to multiple departments (War, Navy, State, White House); the article documents missing records (e.g., 'File 7001' absent) and lack of clear showing in records as to what higher officers in War Department received particular messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights an expectation that receipt/transmission of critical intelligence be recorded and traceable; missing files and unclear records constitute a failure against that standard and impair inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and reliable delivery of vital warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical warnings must be delivered promptly and reliably; the report recounts that a final warning was 'given to a boy for delivery on a bicycle' who was caught in the bombing and did not deliver the message until after the attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an example of breakdowns in delivery mechanisms; implies a standard that sensitive warnings require dependable, secure channels to ensure actionable receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy of communications when primary channels fail
rubrics_metrics.description: When the teletype at Honolulu was not working, the Signal Corps sent messages to San Francisco by Western Union and from there to Hawaii by RCA and the teletype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates expectation of backup channels and procedures to ensure messages get through despite local failures; the article notes this pattern as part of the factual record of what occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and production of intelligence for inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative committees expect that intercepted messages, translations, and related files be preserved and produced; the article notes classified testimony ('top secret') and later placement of an Army board report in the congressional record, and also reports missing files and disappeared records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a standard for transparency to oversight bodies: files should be kept and made available unless legitimately and explicitly withheld; failure to do so fuels controversy and suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. immediate aims for Germany (postwar economic policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State Department set four principal immediate aims for Germany in the period from surrender through the coming winter: (1) increase to the greatest extent the export of coal from Germany to liberated areas; (2) use the months before spring to set up machinery to execute reparations and disarmament programs; (3) ensure sufficient food is available to avoid mass starvation (1,550 calories cited); (4) prevent mass starvation in Germany while not giving Germany higher priority for supplies than other liberated areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These aims are framework criteria guiding occupying authorities in decisions about resources, priorities, and what industrial activity may be permitted or restricted during the immediate postwar interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-stage timeline for German control, reparations, and recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy is organized in three stages: (1) from surrender to at least the end of the present winter (emergency relief and immediate aims), (2) the period of reparations removal running mainly until Feb. 2, 1948, and (3) the final period of German rebuilding and recovery beginning Feb. 2, 1948.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage has distinct objectives (relief and stabilization; reparations/disarmament implementation; eventual restoration of German civilian control and economic recovery) and informs timing for policy measures such as industrial removals and aid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline German diet to prevent mass starvation (1,550 calories/day)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department set a basic ration level for the normal German consumer at 1,550 calories per day to prevent mass starvation this winter; the level could be raised by agreement among the four occupying powers if justified by standards in liberated areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit humanitarian standard used to judge adequacy of food shipments and ration policy; recognizes special higher needs for certain workers (e.g., coal miners) and severe urban shortages (Berlin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle against wanton destruction of peacetime-capable industry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Allies do not intend 'wantonly to destroy German structures and installations which can readily be used for permitted peace-time industrial activities or for temporary purposes' and should avoid destroying facilities usable for civilian industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides decisions about what plants may be removed or destroyed for reparations: preserve facilities that have legitimate peacetime uses; limit destruction to installations directly tied to armament production or those that cannot be removed for reparations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial restrictions to prevent German rearmament
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain specialized armament industries—shipbuilding, aircraft, and certain chemical installations—may be destroyed or restricted because they 'cannot be removed as reparations' and present a risk of diversion to war purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion: identify and remove or disable industries posing rearmament risk while allowing harmless civilian industry to remain; reparations calculation should consider what must be dismantled to prevent future war-making capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reparations withdrawals tied to standard-of-living targets (1948)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reparations withdrawals should be related to a standard of living goal for Germany; the statement sets the 1948 German standard of living target to equal the average standard for Continental Europe (excluding Soviet Union and UK) in 1930-38.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a quantitative policy benchmark linking reparations policy to socio-economic outcomes and limiting reparations to avoid permanently lowering German living standards beyond agreed targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allied financing of essential imports during reparations removal
rubrics_metrics.description: During the reparations removal period the United States and other occupying powers must finance minimum essential imports into Germany to the extent that German exports do not cover the cost of such imports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes an economic-support obligation by occupying powers to prevent collapse and to enable basic subsistence and reparations operations; financing is not seen as reparations but as emergency support tied to organizational disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy against creating a buffer state in Europe
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. officials (Maj. Gen. Hilldring) asserted emphatically that the Western nations had no thought of setting up a 'buffer state' in Europe against Russia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declared diplomatic/political standard shaping occupation policy and territorial planning: the Allies' stated objective is not to rearrange European states to create a buffer but to follow Potsdam principles for rehabilitation.
